_about: Week 3 (synthesis) seed for the Future of Transportation practice project. Replayed by scripts/seed-practice-synthesis.mjs. `implications` are keyed by the Session 2 key change they hang under; `themes` reference tray implications by their exact text.

themes.text: Getting there stops depending on owning or driving a car
themes.description: For people who cannot drive today, travel becomes possible without a licence or a vehicle — as long as service reaches them and they can pay for it.
implications: People who cannot drive today — older adults, people with disabilities, teenagers — can travel alone
Appointment no-show rates fall where rides are reliable and free at the point of use
Fewer people learn to drive
Fewer households own a car, so every trip becomes a purchase decision
People ration trips they would once have taken, including some to care
Food and pharmacy delivery reaches places a store never did
Being unbanked or without a smartphone becomes a barrier to leaving the house
Rural and low-density areas get the thinnest service at exactly the hours shift workers travel
benefit: Older adults, people with disabilities and teenagers can reach work, care and each other without asking someone for a lift.
Clinics see fewer missed appointments wherever the ride is reliable and free at the point of use.
cost: People who are unbanked, phoneless, or outside the app's languages lose the only way the system works.
Households that ration trips by price take fewer of them, and some of those were trips to care.
experience: A rural shift worker reads this as service that is not there at five in the morning.
A parent with three children reads it as three fares rather than one car.
mechanism: Someone has to fund rides as a public service rather than a product, and set a floor on where and when service runs.
The ride has to be bookable without a smartphone, a bank account or English.
risks: Travel becomes something you buy by the trip, so the people with the least money travel least.
A ride you cannot book without a smartphone is not access, however good the coverage map looks.
opportunities: Non-emergency medical transport stops being a separate, under-funded programme and becomes part of the system.
Public health can argue for ride subsidies as a clinical access measure, with attendance data to show for it.

themes.text: The air gets cleaner unevenly, and the new infrastructure lands where it always has
themes.description: Electrification removes the tailpipe, but the vehicles arrive first in the wealthiest neighbourhoods while depots, hubs and substations go where land is cheap.
implications: Tailpipe pollution drops first in the neighbourhoods that get the new vehicles first
Childhood asthma rates diverge between neighbourhoods on the same road network
Charging depots and substations are sited where land is cheap
The communities that hosted the highway now host the grid build-out
Brake, tyre and road-wear particulates stay even after the exhaust goes
Driverless trucks run freight corridors at all hours
Noise and vibration become a night-time sleep problem along those routes
Neighbourhood delivery hubs put industrial activity on residential streets
benefit: Neighbourhoods that get electric fleets early see measurable drops in NO2 and in childhood asthma.
cost: Communities along freight corridors trade exhaust for night-time noise, vibration and a substation.
Anyone whose exposure is brake and tyre particulate sees no improvement at all.
experience: A family on a truck route reads 'clean transportation' as a change in which pollutant keeps them awake.
mechanism: Siting decisions for depots, hubs and substations would have to carry a health review with the standing to say no.
Fleet replacement would have to be scheduled by asthma burden rather than by who buys first.
risks: A city hits its emissions target while the asthma gap inside it widens, and the target is what gets reported.
Noise and sleep loss are not counted, so they are not mitigated.
opportunities: Fleet electrification schedules are a lever public health can ask to see, and to reorder.
Neighbourhood-scale air monitoring becomes cheap enough to be routine rather than a study.

themes.text: Every trip is recorded, and the record is both a tool and a threat
themes.description: Connected infrastructure produces continuous data on who moved where and when. The same record that would transform exposure surveillance is attractive to employers, insurers and enforcement.
implications: Every trip leaves a record of who went where, and when
Movement data becomes attractive to employers, insurers and immigration enforcement
Public health gains near-real-time exposure and mobility data it has never had
One app plans and pays for the whole journey
People without the app, or the languages it speaks, are outside the system
benefit: Public health could see exposure, access and mobility in near real time instead of once a decade.
cost: People with reason to avoid being tracked avoid the system, and then avoid the trip.
Anyone outside the app is invisible in the data as well as outside the service.
experience: The same dataset reads as a public good to an epidemiologist and as a risk register to someone without papers.
mechanism: Clear limits on who may query movement data, for what, with a public record of every request.
A legal basis that survives a change of administration, not a policy that does not.
risks: Public health is handed the data and the reputational cost of how it was collected.
Trust lost to a single enforcement request does not come back.
opportunities: A chance to write the governance rules before the data is routine rather than after.
Exposure surveillance that does not depend on asking people to recall their week.

themes.text: The system gains new single points of failure, and the people least able to absorb them
themes.description: When movement depends on software, a service contract and a working app, an outage is not an inconvenience but a region-wide failure — and the first people stranded are the ones with appointments they cannot miss.
implications: A software fault or outage is now a region-wide transport failure
Dialysis and chemotherapy patients and shift workers are stranded first
Service levels follow demand density rather than need
Rural and low-density areas get the thinnest service at exactly the hours shift workers travel
Transit agencies become buyers of private service rather than operators of their own
The public loses the staff and the standing to set service levels
Driving work disappears as a first rung into the labour market
The health coverage attached to those jobs goes with them
benefit: A system that can be instrumented can also be held to a measurable service standard.
cost: Dialysis patients, shift workers and anyone on a treatment schedule carry the failures.
A workforce that lost driving jobs lost the health coverage attached to them at the same time.
experience: An agency that buys service rather than running it reads an outage as a vendor problem, not a public health emergency.
mechanism: Continuity-of-service requirements written into the procurement contract, with public health at the table when it is written.
A minimum service floor set in public, for hours and places that demand alone would not pay for.
risks: Emergency planning assumes a transport system that nobody in government operates.
By the time an outage happens, there is no public capacity left to run service instead.
opportunities: Transport continuity becomes part of emergency preparedness rather than an afterthought.
Procurement is a public health lever, if we are in the room when it is drafted.

hopesFears.text: We hope that getting to care stops depending on whether someone in the household can drive.
hopesFears.why: Because the appointments people miss are not the ones they do not value, they are the ones they cannot reach.
hopesFears.concerns: Older adults, people with disabilities, and households without a car.

hopesFears.text: We hope that the health effects of a transport decision are visible before the concrete is poured.
hopesFears.why: Because siting is where the next thirty years of asthma and sleep loss get decided, and we are usually told afterwards.
hopesFears.concerns: Communities along freight corridors and near new depots and substations.

hopesFears.text: We fear that clean air arrives as a neighbourhood amenity rather than a public standard.
hopesFears.why: Because a city can meet its emissions target while the gap inside it widens, and the target is what gets reported.
hopesFears.concerns: Low-income neighbourhoods on freight and highway corridors.

flip.text: We hope that the first electric fleets go where the asthma burden is highest, not where the buyers are.
flip.why: Because the same investment can close the gap or widen it, and the order it happens in is the whole decision.

hopesFears.text: We fear that movement data reaches enforcement before it reaches epidemiology.
hopesFears.why: Because the first time a trip record is subpoenaed, the people we most need to reach stop travelling in the system.
hopesFears.concerns: Undocumented residents, people fleeing violence, anyone with reason to avoid a record.

flip.text: We hope that the rules on who may query a trip record are written, public and in force before the data is routine.
flip.why: Because trust is cheaper to keep than to rebuild, and we are early enough to ask.

hopesFears.text: We fear that nobody in government will be able to say what the service level is, let alone change it.
hopesFears.why: Because when agencies buy service instead of running it, an outage becomes a vendor's problem and a patient's emergency.
hopesFears.concerns: Dialysis and chemotherapy patients, shift workers, rural residents.

flip.text: We hope that a minimum service standard is something the public sets and can hold someone to.
flip.why: Because the people who cannot miss a trip are the reason a floor exists at all.

hopesFears.text: We fear that a quieter, emptier street is read as a safer one.
hopesFears.why: Because the street that no longer has traffic noise may also no longer have anybody on it, and isolation does not show up in a crash statistic.
hopesFears.concerns: People living alone, and anyone whose daily contact was incidental.
